awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Diagnostic Solution to Assess Cognitive Decline
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this I-Corps project is based on the development of advanced dementia assessment tools designed to enhance the efficiency of clinical trial patient recruitment and screening processes, thereby accelerating dementia drug development. These tools will enable more precise patient recruitment and reduce screening durations that can currently extend up to 2 years. These advances could lead to a reduction in both the time and cost associated with developing new dementia therapies. This project aims to provide a scalable, robust assistive tool that enables healthcare professionals to assess cognitive health with greater accuracy. Primary care physicians and other healthcare providers can utilize this tool to efficiently and confidently evaluate patients' cognitive status across three major stages and ten etiologies of dementia. By addressing the challenges posed by the shortage of neurological healthcare professionals, the tool facilitates earlier diagnosis and intervention, allowing for more tailored and effective care based on the specific type and stage of dementia.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. The solution is based on the development of a deep learning framework that underpins leading large language models to provide comprehensive probability assessments across various stages of cognitive decline, including normal cognition, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia, as well as across 10 major etiologies, such as Alzheimer's, vascular, and Lewy body diseases. The model leverages a wide range of routine standard-of-care data, including demographic information, patient medical history, neurological tests, images, and genetic data. Beyond its cutting-edge predictive capabilities, this technology incorporates explainable results, enhancing transparency and allowing for the identification of key features influencing each prediction on an individual basis. The solution's diagnostic accuracy meets or exceeds that of experienced clinicians, representing a significant advancement in medical artificial intelligence applications.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Overview and Motivation

 

This project emerged from the National Science Foundation’s I-Corps program to explore how artificial intelligence could help clinicians identify neurological conditions such as dementia earlier and more accurately. Dementia affects over 7 million people in the U.S. today, and that number is projected to grow dramatically as the population ages. Yet, over half of dementia cases remain undiagnosed until late in the disease course, when meaningful intervention is difficult.

 

The project team—based at Boston University and MIT—set out to understand how primary care physicians, neurologists, and healthcare organizations could use existing patient data more effectively to close this diagnostic gap. The work sought to transform the patient journey from one that begins “too late and too broken” to one that enables earlier, proactive care.

 

Project Activities and Findings

 

Through the I-Corps national program, the team conducted more than 100 customer discovery interviews across healthcare systems, research centers, and clinical trial organizations. These interviews revealed that despite major scientific advances in diagnostics, the pathway to care remains largely reactionary. In most cases, patients or their families must first recognize and report cognitive changes before the healthcare system responds, leading to significant delays in assessment and treatment. Primary care physicians, who are best positioned to intervene early, face major obstacles in dementia assessment: limited time, lack of neurological expertise, and fragmented access to test results spread across multiple systems.

 

This customer discovery process highlighted the urgent clinical significance of the problem: when cognitive decline is detected only after noticeable impairment, opportunities for intervention and care planning are severely reduced. Late diagnoses also strain families and increase costs for health systems managing avoidable hospitalizations and institutional care. Clinicians expressed a clear need for tools that could surface risk automatically from existing data and deliver interpretable, workflow-compatible guidance rather than black-box predictions.

 

Building on this feedback, the team developed and validated a web-based AI screening tool—later named Cognimark—that can analyze the same data clinicians already collect (for example, electronic health records, brain imaging, cognitive testing, and lab results) and generate an interpretable report estimating a patient’s likelihood of cognitive impairment. Importantly, the system does not require new or proprietary hardware and can operate even when some data are missing.

 

The I-Corps process also helped uncover a scalable pathway for clinical adoption. Rather than replacing physicians, the technology functions as a neurology “copilot”—flagging at-risk patients directly from health-record data, suggesting confirmatory tests (such as blood-based biomarkers), and routing them to appropriate next steps like specialist referral or clinical trials.

 

 

 

Intellectual Merit

 

Through the National I-Corps program, the project team conducted more than one hundred structured interviews with clinicians, administrators, researchers, and payers to understand the real-world barriers to timely dementia detection.

 

The intellectual contribution of this project lies in converting these stakeholder insights into a scientifically grounded, data-driven framework for earlier neurological assessment. The team combined advances in interpretable machine learning with human-centered design principles inspired by clinician feedback. The resulting approach integrates multimodal patient data—such as electronic health records, imaging, and cognitive testing—to generate transparent, evidence-based reports that mirror clinical reasoning. By grounding the technology in the lived challenges of physicians and patients, this work advances both the field of explainable artificial intelligence and its practical application in healthcare delivery.

 

Broader Impacts

 

The broader impact of this project lies in improving access to neurological care and reducing the societal and economic burden of dementia, which exceeds $1 trillion annually worldwide. By helping clinicians detect disease earlier, Cognimark’s approach can enable timely intervention—potentially delaying institutional care and lowering healthcare costs by thousands of dollars per patient per year.

 

The project also strengthened the regional innovation ecosystem by training scientists and engineers at the intersection of neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and entrepreneurship. Through I-Corps, the team learned to translate academic research into a practical product, forming collaborations with community health systems, clinical-trial sponsors, and patient-advocacy groups.

 

The spinout company Cognimark Inc., now based in Boston, continues to develop the technology with support from Boston University, MIT, and industry advisors from Columbia University and Harvard Business School. The company’s early deployments with physician practices and clinical-trial networks have already analyzed tens of thousands of patient records, demonstrating feasibility in real clinical environments.

 

Conclusion

 

The NSF I-Corps program played a pivotal role in bridging academic research and real-world healthcare application. What began as a scientific exploration of AI for Alzheimer’s disease evolved—through customer engagement and market discovery—into a platform that helps clinicians act sooner, patients receive care earlier, and health systems manage costs more effectively.

 

By enabling faster, data-driven neurological assessment using information that already exists in medical records, the project advances both the intellectual merit of interpretable AI and the broader societal goal of equitable, proactive brain-health care.
